doc.title: Clay Jenkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 18, 2016

title: Leaving space on a Joe LaBarbera recording
summary: Jenkins discusses his habit of leaving space, soloing with Bob Sheppard and Bill Cunliffe, and praises Joe LaBarbera.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Okay. Here’s — this actually starts with some piano.
Yeah. That was probably Bill Cunliffe on piano.
Yeah. So I wanted to ask you about what happened there. Because of course in the whole recording there’s the head and then I think the sax player plays.
Bob Sheppard. Then there’s this piano solo. And it gets pretty intense. And then you come in and there’s a lot of space. And I’m wondering, I was thinking how deliberate and how preplanned was that?

I wouldn’t say preplanned at all, because I always leave a lot of space. I’ve had people say, “man I like the way you leave space.” Sometimes if they compliment me it’s because of the space I leave. Pete Erskine said that to me one time, he said, “I like how you leave space.” So to me it just helps me listen to them and maybe I can kind of — not that I want them to copy me or mark me or anything like that, but it also gives me ideas when I leave space. Like with Joe, Joe never repeats what I play but it’s just like a momentum gathering thing to leave space with Joe. Because he’s such a fantastic drummer. And I’ve always left a lot of space. And I leave more space than a lot of guys — and I try to get my students to leave space. Now sometimes, with some players, space is long notes. Like with Trane or with Rich Perry. He’s another tenor player who I love. Rich Perry is one of my favorite tenor players. Rich doesn’t leave a ton of space but his space is long notes. So that’s when things start churning. But for me I like to leave big gaping holes of space.
Well it gives you somewhere to go too.
It does. Yeah. And it makes me listen. Yeah.

And I felt like for that particular recording that the other players were sort of responding to you. Like the piano player sort of laid out for a while, like I’m not going to mess with what he’s doing too much, the best thing I can do is not play for the time being.

And he knows I will travel far and wide to get to play with Joe LaBarbera. Because Joe is one of the most amazing people, and amazing drummer. And he loves to play. And he makes people play better, which is the biggest compliment I can say for anybody. I’ve gotten to play with some really great drummers. He and Jeff Hamilton and Dennis Mackrel and Steve Houghton, and all these great drummers I’ve gotten to play with. The guy at Eastman, Rich Thompson. They make you play better. Joe is amazing.
Joe is out in Los Angeles.
